title: Distribution, Supply Chain & Unit Economics
book_title: Chapter 3: How It Is Sold & Delivered — Distribution & Unit Economics

epigraph.quote: “Extended Payment Cycles from Developers: Cash strapped real estate developers might extend payment cycles which further can impact procurement and fabrication.”
epigraph.author: Aluwind Infra-Tech, Annual Report FY2025-26, Management Discussion and Analysis (threats)

web_blocks.caption: Audited consolidated FY2026 waterfall from the annual-report financial statements; ₹ crore inputs, scaled to ₹100 of revenue. Cost of goods is cost of materials consumed (₹101.71 Cr) plus stock-in-trade purchases (₹0.29 Cr) less the ₹5.03 Cr build in finished goods and work in progress; capex is purchase of fixed and intangible assets; tax is the profit-and-loss charge.
web_blocks.takeaway: Of every ₹100 of sales, ₹7.54 reached profit after tax, but operating cash flow was −₹11.79 and capex took another ₹3.23, leaving free cash flow near −₹15.01 per ₹100.

web_blocks.html: Aluwind reaches customers through four routes. A developer or contractor floats a tender, Aluwind’s sales team has usually pitched the architect or consultant earlier, and the contract goes to a pre-qualified bidder. The prospectus says customers limit the tender to contractors they have pre-qualified on net worth, experience, capacity, safety record, financial strength and bonding capacity, but “price competitiveness of the bid is the most important selection criterion” [3]. The company also claims an 80% repeat-client rate and says many orders come from one-to-one negotiation with existing clients [3]. Offices are in Malad and Goregaon in Mumbai and in Pune, with the Pune experience centre serving as showroom [3]. Orders in Chennai, Coimbatore, Madurai and Ahmedabad show the push beyond Maharashtra, and management names Karnataka, Gujarat and Telangana next; Ajay Porwal was hired on 5 November 2026 to explore exports [7][12][5].

web_blocks.takeaway: Most revenue comes through tenders won on price against pre-qualification, so Aluwind sets neither the price nor the payment terms. The Eternia channel gives access and brand, at the cost of dependence on one supplier.

web_blocks.html: Supply chain is the next constraint. The core materials are glass, aluminium profiles, ACP, mild steel, galvanised sheet, sealants, gaskets and hardware, sourced locally and abroad [3]. Hindalco supplied 34% of FY22 purchases, 44% of FY23 and 30% of H1 FY24, with glass from Sejal, Jajoo and FG Glass and extrusions from Ramco and Jindal Aluminium in the top ten [3]. The prospectus says the company has no long-term supply agreements and buys mostly on the spot market [3]. It also says contracts usually carry escalation and delay-charge clauses and that the company recovers cost increases from customers [3], but the FY26 accounting policy says it signs fixed-price contracts [1], and the FY26 results release cites commodity volatility as a headwind [2]. The aluminium price-variation clause, if any, is not disclosed, and I treat price risk as largely the company’s own. Larger raw-material and stores balances (₹44.4 Cr against ₹22.4 Cr a year earlier) may reflect early buying, which would be a hedge as well as a cash cost; the filing does not say [1]. The Italian five-axis CNC machine, a computer-controlled cutter that can machine all faces of a profile in one setup, drove the FY26 foreign-exchange outgo of ₹2.78 Cr; no foreign-currency exposure remained at year end [8][1].

The Pune plant is where the economics are decided. In June 2025 the company stated capacity of 18,600 m² a month at 50% utilisation, plus 3,162 m² from a new CNC line costing ₹3.90 Cr, which it expected to be fully used from H2 FY26 [9]. That makes a rated 21,762 m² a month, about 261,000 m² a year, against 160,368 m² a year and 65,378 m² produced in FY23 [3]. FY26 utilisation is not disclosed. Employees rose from 178 permanent staff in September 2023 to over 500 in March 2026 [3][1]. Site installers are hired through labour contractors on contract rather than subcontracting whole projects [3]. Labour and factory cost was ₹23.27 Cr in FY26, 16.8% of revenue, against ₹15.01 Cr or 13.7% in FY25 [1]. Plant is light: net block is ₹9.59 Cr against ₹138.56 Cr of sales, so capital intensity sits in working capital, not in machines.

Contract terms turn that into cash timing. Revenue follows the percentage-of-completion method, in which sales are recognised as cost is incurred against total estimated cost [1]. Customers hold retention money, a slice of each bill held back until the defect-liability period ends, and contractors usually furnish performance bank guarantees and bear liquidated damages for delay [3]. At March 2026 retention receivable was ₹13.68 Cr, up from ₹9.82 Cr, while retention payable to vendors was only ₹1.69 Cr [1]. Advances received on live contracts fell from ₹9.50 Cr to ₹5.78 Cr, so customers financed less of the work [1]. Unbilled revenue, work done but not yet invoiced, was ₹32.75 Cr. Together billed receivables, retention and unbilled work came to ₹71.80 Cr, 52% of revenue, against ₹55.67 Cr or 51% a year earlier [1]. Contract cost incurred on live projects was ₹206.92 Cr with ₹23.82 Cr of recognised profit, an 11.5% margin on cost [1].

Use the audited consolidated FY2026 accounts to follow ₹100 of revenue. Materials, stock changes and construction inputs used ₹69.98. Employee cost used ₹12.29 and other expenses ₹5.90. That leaves an EBITDA of ₹11.83, or ₹16.39 Cr. Depreciation took ₹1.26 and interest ₹1.56; other income added ₹1.11; tax took ₹2.58. Profit after tax was ₹7.54 per ₹100, or ₹10.45 Cr [1]. Operating profit before working-capital changes was ₹16.93 Cr, ₹12.22 per ₹100. Then working capital absorbed ₹30.04 Cr, ₹21.68 per ₹100. Inventory took ₹27.02 Cr, receivables and unbilled work ₹16.13 Cr, and the fall in customer advances and other liabilities ₹3.69 Cr; suppliers financed ₹14.36 Cr, and vendor advances and other assets released a net ₹2.44 Cr [1].

Why was operating cash flow negative? The statement’s “net cash flow used in operating activities” is ₹16.33 Cr negative for FY26 and ₹18.85 Cr negative for FY25, consolidated, after ₹3.23 Cr of tax paid, and before interest (₹2.16 Cr), which sits in financing [1]. Cash generated from operations was −₹13.11 Cr. The standalone figure is −₹16.31 Cr, and the H1 FY27 filing restates the FY26 comparative as −₹16.32 Cr; I use the audited consolidated figure, and Screener’s “−16” rounds the same number [1][5][6]. The cause is straightforward. Profit is booked as work progresses, but cash arrives when customers pay. Inventory grew 88% (₹30.54 Cr to ₹57.56 Cr, with stores and spares up from ₹5.05 Cr to ₹13.81 Cr) against 27% revenue growth, and customers owed more while advancing less. A growing contractor therefore consumes cash even while profitable, unless billing is front-loaded or suppliers lend.

web_blocks.takeaway: Debtor days beat the plan; inventory days are two to three and a half times the plan, and suppliers carry four to six times the planned credit period. The cycle rose from 126 to 181 days in a year on the Screener basis. The prospectus uses cost of materials as the base; Screener uses sales and purchases; the AR ratios use average balances, so only the direction is comparable [3][6][1].

web_blocks.html: The same number is visible in the balance sheet. Supplier credit rose from ₹25.71 Cr to ₹40.07 Cr, of which ₹7.49 Cr is covered by letters of credit, a bank undertaking that pays the supplier [1]. Borrowings rose from ₹13.09 Cr to ₹41.32 Cr. The facilities are cash credit of ₹10 Cr with ICICI and ₹15 Cr with Kotak at 8.15%, a ₹10 Cr working-capital demand loan, and ₹9.11 Cr of unsecured bank and NBFC loans at 8.15% to 13.50%, backed by personal guarantees from three Kabra directors and, for ICICI, a relative, and by mortgages on the Malad office, a Mumbai flat and the Pune factory [1]. About ₹12.64 Cr of deposits are under bank lien, so part of the borrowing is sitting in security rather than funding work [1]. The cash-conversion arithmetic is a fair reading of how the business works: the order book of about ₹300 Cr converts to revenue only as fast as the plant, the site crews and the customers’ payments allow [2].

H1 FY27 shows the direction but not yet the cure. Operating cash flow turned to +₹0.81 Cr, because inventory fell ₹6.18 Cr to ₹51.38 Cr. Billed receivables rose ₹15.65 Cr to ₹54.70 Cr, supplier credit fell ₹3.50 Cr and borrowings rose to ₹46.06 Cr; plant spending was ₹1.74 Cr [5]. I would put the odds of FY27 operating cash flow turning clearly positive (above ₹5 Cr) at about 35%, because it needs receivables to flatten while the promised second-half revenue ramp arrives. The next chapter takes up the risks that follow.

book_paragraphs: Walk with me for a moment to a shed at Gat 374 on the Pune-Aurangabad highway at Koregaon Bhima. Aluminium sections arrive in bundles, many of them from Hindalco, the maker of Eternia [3]. In one corner a seven-tank pretreatment line cleans them before a powder-coating booth and oven paint them [3]. In another, computer-controlled cutters and a new Italian five-axis machine cut and machine each profile with the precision a window or a unitised panel demands [8]. Finished frames are loaded on the company’s own vehicles and driven to a tower in Mumbai or a campus in Chennai. That is the whole physical business. The shed is not where the hard part is.

The hard part is how an order gets there. Aluwind does not sell from a shelf. A developer or contractor floats a tender, an architect or consultant has often already been briefed, and Aluwind bids. The prospectus is candid about the rules. Clients shortlist bidders on net worth, experience, capacity and bonding, but then, in the company’s own words, “price competitiveness of the bid is the most important selection criterion” [3]. Many orders come back from clients it has served before; management speaks of an 80% repeat rate [3]. That matters because it means relationships get Aluwind onto the list, and price decides the winner.

There are four routes. For façades, the company usually works as a subcontractor to a main contractor such as L&T Construction or Vascon Engineers. For windows, it often deals directly with developers such as Godrej, Runwal, Lodha and Tata Realty. The third route is Eternia, the Hindalco window brand: Aluwind is its lead partner in the Mumbai region, and that agreement comes up for renewal in December 2026 [3][4]. The fourth is a new toll arrangement, under which Aluwind builds Eternia’s retail window orders for a fee [2]. It earned ₹1.57 Cr from that in FY26. Look at what is common to the first three: Aluwind does not set the price and does not set the payment terms.

Now follow the money. The raw materials are glass, aluminium sections, panels, steel, sealants, gaskets and hardware [3]. There are no long-term supply contracts; most is bought on the spot market [3]. The prospectus says contracts usually allow for cost escalation and that the company recovers price rises from customers, yet the FY26 accounting policy says contracts are fixed price, and the company itself lists aluminium volatility among its threats [3][1]. If there is an aluminium price-variation clause, it is not disclosed. Until I see one, I assume Aluwind carries a good part of the metal-price risk between the day it bids and the day it buys.

Capacity first, then people. In June 2025 the company stated 18,600 m² a month at 50% utilisation and added 3,162 m² a month with a ₹3.90 Cr CNC line [9]. Rated capacity is therefore about 21,762 m² a month, or roughly 261,000 m² a year, against 65,378 m² produced in FY23 [3]. It has not said how full the plant is today. The staff has grown from 178 permanent employees in 2023 to over 500 in March 2026, and site crews come through labour contractors [3][1]. Labour and factory cost rose from 13.7% of sales to 16.8% in a year [1]. Plant and machinery is small, with a net block of ₹9.59 Cr against sales of ₹138.56 Cr. So the money in this business is not in the shed. It is in the stock and the unpaid bills.

The contract terms decide when the cash arrives. Revenue is booked as work progresses, by comparing cost incurred with estimated total cost [1]. Customers keep back a slice of every bill as retention until the defect period ends. The contractor usually has to furnish a performance bank guarantee, which a customer can call if the work fails, and pays liquidated damages if it is late [3]. None of the billing schedules is disclosed. What is disclosed is the result: ₹32.75 Cr of unbilled work, ₹13.68 Cr of retention and ₹25.37 Cr of ordinary receivables at March 2026 [1].

Let me show you where each ₹100 of FY26 revenue went, using the audited consolidated accounts. Materials and stock changes took ₹69.98. Employees took ₹12.29. Other expenses took ₹5.90. That leaves an EBITDA of ₹11.83, or ₹16.39 Cr. Depreciation took ₹1.26, interest ₹1.56 and tax ₹2.58, while other income added ₹1.11. Profit after tax was ₹7.54, or ₹10.45 Cr [1]. If the story ended there, you would call it a decent business. It does not end there.

Because the second page of the accounts, the cash flow statement, says that the operating cash flow was minus ₹16.33 Cr [1]. Let me be precise about what that number is. It is the audited consolidated net cash flow from operating activities, after ₹3.23 Cr of tax paid and before ₹2.16 Cr of interest, which the company reports under financing. Before working capital the business generated ₹16.93 Cr. Then it spent ₹30.04 Cr on working capital. Inventory took ₹27.02 Cr. Customers and unbilled work took ₹16.13 Cr. Customer advances and other liabilities fell by ₹3.69 Cr. Suppliers lent ₹14.36 Cr to help, and vendor advances and other items returned a net ₹2.44 Cr. The result: minus ₹13.11 Cr from operations, and minus ₹16.33 Cr after tax. Per ₹100 of sales, that is a cash loss of ₹11.79. After ₹4.47 Cr of capital spending, free cash flow was minus ₹20.80 Cr, minus ₹15.01 per ₹100. (The standalone figure is −₹16.31 Cr, and the H1 FY27 filing shows the FY26 comparative as −₹16.32 Cr. I use the audited consolidated number.) [1][5]

Why did it happen? Think of a contractor who must buy aluminium and glass, build the panels, and hang them, before the customer’s final cheque. Inventory grew 88%, from ₹30.54 Cr to ₹57.56 Cr, while revenue grew 27%. Stores and spares alone went from ₹5.05 Cr to ₹13.81 Cr, and the filing does not say what is in that bucket [1]. Customers held ₹13.68 Cr of retention, up from ₹9.82 Cr, while Aluwind held back only ₹1.69 Cr from its own vendors [1]. Advances from customers fell from ₹9.50 Cr to ₹5.78 Cr, so the customers funded less of the work [1]. Billed receivables, retention and unbilled work together were ₹71.80 Cr, 52% of revenue [1]. A growing contractor eats cash even while earning profit, unless customers pay in advance or suppliers lend.

Suppliers did lend. Trade payables rose from ₹25.71 Cr to ₹40.07 Cr, of which ₹7.49 Cr is covered by bank letters of credit [1]. And the banks lent too: borrowings went from ₹13.09 Cr to ₹41.32 Cr, through cash credit lines of ₹10 Cr and ₹15 Cr, a ₹10 Cr working-capital loan and ₹9.11 Cr of unsecured bank and NBFC money, with the cash-credit lines backed by personal guarantees from the Kabra brothers [1]. About ₹12.64 Cr of deposits sit under bank lien, so part of what was borrowed is parked as security [1].

Let me put the promise and the outcome next to each other, as I did in Chapter 1. The prospectus planned for debtors of 114 days, inventory of 72 days and suppliers paid in 29 days, a cycle of about 157 days [3]. The filings show debtor days of 103 on one basis and 90 on another, better than planned. Inventory days of 258 or 167 are far worse than planned. Payable days of 180 or 118 are far longer than planned. On the Screener basis the full cycle went from 126 to 181 days in one year [6]. On the company’s own turnover ratios it is about 139 days [1]. Pick either basis: the cash is trapped for four to six months, and suppliers are carrying more of it than the company said they would.

H1 FY27 offers a first sign of change and a warning. Operating cash flow turned slightly positive at ₹0.81 Cr, because inventory fell ₹6.18 Cr [5]. But billed receivables rose by ₹15.65 Cr to ₹54.70 Cr, supplier credit fell by ₹3.50 Cr and borrowings reached ₹46.06 Cr [5]. I would give about a 35% chance that FY27 operating cash flow ends clearly positive, above ₹5 Cr. It needs receivables to flatten just as the second-half revenue ramp arrives. The risks that follow are the subject of the next chapter.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Aluwind’s plant is small and its margins are fine; its problem is the clock. Every rupee of new revenue has to be financed for about four to six months by stock, unbilled work and withheld retention, and the funding so far has come from suppliers and banks. Do not judge a contractor by what it earns on a job. Judge it by when the last rupee of that job reaches the bank.
